transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Yeah, um, so what finally made me come in is that I keep making these really small but super embarrassing mistakes on things. Like, I've been turning in job applications and my research notes, and I'll realize later that I completely mislabeled an artwork date or just skipped a question entirely. Which is wild because I honestly thought I had checked them. I swear I look them over. 

I actually just finished my bachelor's in art history, which was a lot of reading and dates, obviously. The department at my school had this incredible archive of Renaissance prints that I got to work with. Have you ever seen how they do lithography? It's actually fascinating, they use this special heavy limestone and you have to keep it perfectly wet with a sponge while you ink it, otherwise the whole image gets ruined. I really wanted to take a studio class on it, but the waitlist was always miles long... 

Wait, sorry. What was I saying? Oh, right, the applications. But yeah, I keep sending them out with those little skipped questions or wrong dates even when I swear I proofread them, and it's just getting really frustrating trying to find a job when that keeps happening.
Looking back at your childhood or your time in elementary school, did you experience these same kinds of struggles with attention, organization, or making careless mistakes?

Yeah, actually, it’s kind of always been a thing. Like, even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I had really good ideas, but I just... forgot to turn in my worksheets. Or I’d completely lose the instructions for projects. 

I remember this one project in fourth grade, we had to make a diorama of a Native American longhouse, and I spent hours gathering real twigs and bark from my backyard to make it look authentic. I even used this air-dry clay to make tiny little fire pits. Working with clay is actually what got me into art in the first place, I think. There’s something really satisfying about the tactile nature of it, you know? Like how you have to wedge it to get the air bubbles out before you throw it on a wheel, otherwise the whole piece just explodes in the kiln. We had a kiln at my high school that broke down constantly... 

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, childhood. But yeah, I was always missing little details like that. Honestly, the only reason I survived elementary school was because my parents checked my backpack every single night to make sure my homework actually made it out of my folders.
When you were in school, did you often find it difficult to stay seated or feel like you had to be constantly moving?

No, not really. I've never been the type to bounce off the walls or anything. I mean, I can sit still just fine. I actually prefer sitting, especially when I'm reading or, you know, looking at art books. I have this one massive hardcover book on the Dutch Golden Age that weighs like ten pounds. It's gorgeous, though. The reproduction quality on the Vermeer paintings is unbelievable. You can actually see the little cracks in the paint, the craquelure, I think it's called? It's wild to think about how they ground their own pigments back then, like using real lapis lazuli for blue. Lapis is so expensive now, I can't even imagine... 

Um, but yeah, no, sitting still isn't the issue. I just sort of... zone out while I'm sitting there.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others while they are speaking or blurting out answers before a question has been fully asked?

No, I don't really do that. I'm usually pretty quiet in conversations, actually. I'm more of a listener, I guess. Or, well, I try to be. Sometimes I'm listening, but then someone will mention something, and my brain just kind of... goes somewhere else. Like the other day, my friend was telling me about this new coffee shop she went to, and she mentioned they had these ceramic mugs that looked hand-thrown, and suddenly I was just thinking about this exhibit I saw last year on Japanese tea bowls. The wabi-sabi aesthetic is so interesting, how they actually value the imperfections in the glaze. There was this one bowl from the 16th century that had this incredible ash glaze that looked almost like melted glass pooling at the bottom... 

Oh, sorry. What did you ask me? Right, interrupting. Yeah, no, I don't really blurt things out or talk over people. If anything, I probably take too long to answer because I'm trying to catch back up to what they were saying.
In your daily life, do you find it difficult to keep your personal belongings, workspace, or schedule organized?

Yeah, definitely. Both my apartment and my laptop basically just look like a graveyard of half-started projects. It’s just... rent papers, gallery notes, article PDFs, and to-do lists scattered literally everywhere. 

Speaking of the PDFs, I was reading this one yesterday about the restoration of the Sistine Chapel ceiling. It’s actually wild how much soot and grime built up over the centuries just from candles burning in there. They used this special solvent to clean it, but some art historians are still super mad about it because they argue it removed Michelangelo's original second layer of paint—the a secco layer, where he added all the shadows and details after the fresco dried. It’s this massive controversy in the conservation world, and I spent like three hours yesterday just going down a rabbit hole about chemical solvents used in the 1980s... 

Wait, sorry. Organizing. Right. But yeah, because everything is just everywhere all at once, I have a really hard time figuring out what actually needs to happen first. So nothing really gets put away.
Do you often feel a sense of inner restlessness or an internal need to be doing something, even if you are able to sit still physically?

Um, no, I don't think so. I don't really get that restless, driven-by-a-motor feeling. My mind wanders a lot, obviously, but it’s not an anxious or uncomfortable energy. I actually really appreciate stillness. I think that's why I'm so drawn to still life paintings, honestly. The traditional nature morte stuff where time is just entirely frozen. 

There’s this one 17th-century Flemish painter, Clara Peeters, and she was one of the very first artists to do those hyper-realistic banquet pieces. She would actually paint these microscopic self-portraits of her own face reflected in the curved metal of the goblets and jugs on the table. It is absolutely incredible when you look at the high-res scans. And they almost always feature those half-peeled lemons with the rind spiraling down, which was this massive luxury item back then, but also a vanitas symbol to remind you that life is beautiful but bitter. The whole concept of painting decaying fruit and flies just to remind rich people about their own mortality is so fascinating... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Restless? Right, yeah. No, I don't feel that internal need to be moving or doing things. I can just sit totally still for hours looking at things like that without feeling like I need to get up.
